AI Adoption and Data-Related Jobs in the US
text:
The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, including Machine Learning, Generative Adversarial Networks, and Generative AI is rapidly transforming the job market. And while these advancements offer new opportunities, diversions and entertainment for my students, they also pose significant challenges for them as they graduate and continue on to college, trade school, the military, or the workforce. As a result, many students and parents are; essentially, freaking out:
“Mr Barron….are we cooked?”
As a high school teacher of Economics and Business Studies, I get asked some version of this question at least 5 times a day. This is often followed up with discussions of which jobs, careers, and college majors are “AI proof” or at least somewhat protected from the oncoming wave of automation that appears inevitable to my students.
Short answer…no, we are not cooked. But we are in a period of rapid change, and the future of work is uncertain. This study aims to explore the skills and knowledge that you will need to thrive in a world where AI is increasingly prevalent. By analyzing current trends, educational resources, and industry demands, we will provide actionable insights to help you prepare for the evolving job market.

title: AI Adoption and Data-Related Jobs in the US
text:
What are we investigating?
The goal of this investigation is to examine whether AI adoption and related technology and economic signals are reflected in labor-market demand. In order to measure labor market demand on a scale closer to real time, we use the following three labor market series based on Indeed Job openings as a proxy:

Data Analytics job openings
Software job openings
Overall job openings

AI adoption metrics also proved difficult to pin down as there is no universal measurement. For proxies we looked at Capital Expenditure (CAPEX), NVIDIA’s monthly revenues for AI chips, and Token Prices (TPI). Although there was no direct signal for AI Adoption, we were able to combine labor-market data with measures of public interest, technology investment, financial markets, and broader economic conditions to examine whether these signals help explain changes in Data Analytics, Software, and overall job openings.

Official Research Questions

Primary Research Question (RQ1): How has the adoption of AI affected the types of skills employers request in entry level job postings.
Potential Secondary Research Question (RQ2): To what extent do these entry level skill requirements vary across different industries?

title: AI Adoption and Data-Related Jobs in the US
text:
Methodology
We first explore the relationships between job openings and external technology and economic indicators. We then use traditional time-series and deep learning models to forecast job-opening trends and compare their forecasting performance. Future work will extend the analysis to job descriptions to examine how AI-related skill demand changes over time.

title: AI Adoption and Data-Related Jobs in the US
text:
Initial Literature Review

I. AI and Technological Change in the Labor Market
Canaries in the Coal Mine: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market
Authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
Core Finding: The paper documents six facts characterizing labor market shifts following the widespread adoption of generative AI:

Since the widespread adoption of generative AI, early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations have experienced a 16 percent relative decline in employment even after controlling for firm-level shocks
Overall employment continues to grow robustly, but employment growth for young workers has been stagnant since late 2022
Entry-level employment has declined in applications of AI that automate work, but not those that most augment it
Employment declines for young, AI-exposed workers remain after conditioning on firm-time effects such as interest rate changes
The labor market adjustments are visible in employment more than in compensation.
The results are not driven solely by computer occupations or by occupations susceptible to remote work and outsourcing.

How it informs my project:

Facts 1 and 3 are particularly relevant to our project, as they suggest that the adoption of AI has had a significant impact on the employment prospects of young workers in certain occupations. This aligns with our primary research question, which seeks to understand how AI adoption has affected the types of skills employers request in entry-level job postings.
This will be tested using the Cross Price Elasticity of Demand (XED) metric, which measures the responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a one good or service to a change in the pricem of a another good In this case, we can use XED to measure the responsiveness of entry-level job postings to changes in AI adoption (via the proxy of NVIDIA AI Chip revenues) making a distinction between all entry jobs, Data analytics jobs, and software engineering related positions.



II. AI Exposure Across Occupations
Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
Authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory; Anthropic
Core Findings:

AI is far from reaching its theoretical capability: actual coverage remains a fraction of what’s feasible
Occupations with higher observed exposure are projected by the BLS to grow less through 2034
Workers in the most exposed professions are more likely to be older, female, more educated, and higher-paid
No systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022, though we find suggestive evidence that hiring of younger workers has slowed in exposed occupations

How it informs our project:

We will compare and contrast the effects of AI adoption on highly exposed occupations (software and data analytics job postings) to all job postings.



III. Job Postings and Skill Demand:
Automation, artificial intelligence and future skills needs: an Irish perspective
Authors: Raimunda Bukartaite and Daire Hooper
Core Finding:
The accelerated pace of technological change is leading to evolving skill demands across all workforce sectors. While STEM skills are often prioritized, soft skills like collaboration and critical thinking are also crucial for bridging the skill gap and effectively adopting advanced technologies.

How it informs our project:

Using NLP (Natural Language Processing), we will look for patterns in the key skills mentioned in “entry level” job postings on Google Jobs in the US over the last 5 years.



IV. Economic and Technology Indicators:
Automation, artificial intelligence and future skills needs: an Irish perspective
Authors: Raimunda Bukartaite and Daire Hooper
Core Finding:
The accelerated pace of technological change is leading to evolving skill demands across all workforce sectors. While STEM skills are often prioritized, soft skills like collaboration and critical thinking are also crucial for bridging the skill gap and effectively adopting advanced technologies.
How it informs our project:

Using NLP (Natural Language Processing), we will look for patterns in the key skills mentioned in “entry level” job postings on Google Jobs in the US over the last 5 years.



V. Forecasting Economic Trends:
Data-driven workforce forecasting for transportation infrastructure: A comparative analysis of deep learning and statistical time series models
Authors: Adedolapo Ogungbire,
Suman Kumar Mitra, & Sarah Hernandez
Core Finding:

1-D CNN outperforms ARIMA and LSTM in workforce forecasting accuracy.
1-D CNN delivers stable forecasts for both short- and long-term horizons.
ARIMA shows strong short-term stability but weak long-term adaptability.

How it informs our project:

We will compare the performance of 3 traditional models (ARIMA, ARIMAX, & SARIMA) with 3 Deep Learning models (RNN, LSTM, & GRU) in predicting job postings using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).



VI. Literature Review Conclusions:
Existing research has examined AI exposure, employment trends, occupational skill demand, and labor-market forecasting. Our project attempts to bring these areas together by combining job-opening data with technology-related and economic indicators and comparing traditional time-series and deep learning approaches. Future work will extend the analysis to job descriptions using Natural Language Processing (NLP) to investigate how AI-related skill demand is changing over time.

text:
Important Note
These data sources do not directly measure AI adoption by themselves. Instead, they provide useful indicators of the labor market and industries most closely connected to data, software, cloud computing, and information services. We will combine these sources with Google Trends and other AI-related indicators to better understand changes in demand for data-related jobs.

title: Data Sources
section: Indeed Job Posting Indexes from FRED
text:
Indeed Job Posting Indexes from FRED
The Indeed job-posting series are useful because they measure changes in online job postings over time. These series are indexed to a pre-pandemic baseline, which makes it easier to compare overall job posting activity with data-related or technology-related job categories.

Overall Job Postings
Job Postings on Indeed in the United States
This source gives an overall measure of job posting activity in the United States. In the project, we can use this as a baseline to compare whether data-related or technology-related job postings are increasing or decreasing faster than the overall labor market.


Software Development Job Postings
Software Development Job Postings on Indeed in the United States
This source is one of the most relevant for the project because software development is closely connected to AI, data science, machine learning, and automation. We can use this series to examine whether software-related job postings changed during the period of rapid AI adoption.


IT Operations and Helpdesk Job Postings
IT Operations and Helpdesk Job Postings on Indeed in the United States
This source can help us compare technical support and IT operations demand with software development demand. It may show whether AI adoption is affecting different technology-related job areas in different ways.


Mathematics Job Postings
Mathematics Job Postings on Indeed in the United States
This source is useful because many data-related careers depend on quantitative and analytical skills. We can use this series as a proxy for demand in math-heavy roles, including analytics, modeling, statistics, and data science.


Scientific Research and Development Job Postings
Scientific Research and Development Job Postings on Indeed in the United States
This source can help us examine demand in research-oriented jobs. Since AI is increasingly used in scientific research, this series may provide useful context for how research and technical job markets are changing.

title: Data Sources
section: Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services
text:
Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services
These sources focus on the data-processing, hosting, cloud infrastructure, and information-services industry. This industry is highly relevant to AI adoption because AI systems depend on data storage, computing infrastructure, cloud platforms, and digital services.

GDP: Data Processing, Hosting, and Other Information Services
Gross Domestic Product: Data Processing, Hosting, and Other Information Services
This source measures the economic output of the data-processing and hosting industry. In the project, we can use it to examine whether the economic size of this industry has grown alongside the rise of AI, cloud computing, and data-driven services.


Employment: Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web Hosting, and Related Services
All Employees, Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web Hosting, and Related Services
This source measures employment in the computing infrastructure and data-processing industry. It can help us study whether employment in this AI-adjacent industry has grown, declined, or changed over time.


Employment: Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services
Employment for Information: Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services
This source provides another employment measure for the data-processing and hosting industry. We can compare this with job-posting trends to see whether job postings and actual employment move in similar directions.


Total Revenue: Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services
Total Revenue for Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services
This source measures revenue in the data-processing and hosting industry. It can help us examine whether the business activity of data-related services has increased during the period when AI tools and cloud-based systems became more widely used.


Producer Price Index: Data Processing and Related Services
Producer Price Index by Industry: Data Processing and Related Services
This source measures price changes for data-processing and related services. It can be used to study whether the cost or pricing of data-related services has changed over time, especially as demand for cloud computing, data infrastructure, and AI-related services grows.

title: Data Sources
text:
Google Trends Data
Google Trends data will be used to measure public interest in AI-related jobs and skills in the United States. These data do not measure actual job openings, but they help us understand when people became more interested in AI careers, data science careers, and technical skills.
Possible search terms include job-related terms such as “AI jobs,” “data science jobs,” “machine learning jobs,” “AI engineer,” and “ML engineer,” as well as skill-related terms such as “Python,” “LLM,” “generative AI,” “AI agents,” “deep learning,” and “RAG system.”
In this project, we will compare Google Trends patterns with FRED and Indeed job-posting indicators. This will help us examine whether public interest in AI and data-related topics increased before, during, or after changes in software development, mathematics, scientific research, and data-processing job indicators.

title: Data Sources
section: How Google Trends Will Be Used in the Project
text:
How Google Trends Will Be Used in the Project
Google Trends data will be used as a measure of public interest in AI-related jobs and skills. We can compare search interest in job terms such as “AI jobs,” “data science jobs,” and “machine learning jobs” with search interest in skill terms such as “Python,” “LLM,” “generative AI,” and “deep learning.” These trends can then be compared with FRED and Indeed job-posting data to examine whether public interest and labor-market indicators appear to move together over time.

AI and Data-Related Job Search Interest
AI jobs
This source shows search interest in the term “AI jobs” in the United States. It can be used to examine whether public interest in AI-related employment increased during the period when AI tools became more widely used.
Data science jobs
This source shows search interest in “data science jobs.” In the project, we can compare this trend with job-posting indicators to see whether public interest in data science careers moves together with labor-market demand.
Machine learning jobs
This source shows search interest in “machine learning jobs.” It can help us understand whether interest in machine learning careers increased as AI and automation became more common in industry.
Generative AI
This source captures search interest in “generative AI.” Since generative AI became more visible after tools such as ChatGPT became popular, this trend can help us examine whether public attention to AI increased sharply in recent years.
AI engineer
This source shows search interest in the term “AI engineer.” It can be useful for studying whether newer AI-specific job titles are becoming more visible to the public.
ML engineer
This source shows search interest in “ML engineer,” a common role connected to machine learning and applied AI. We can compare this trend with “AI engineer” and “data science jobs” to see how interest in different career paths changes over time.


AI and Data-Related Skill Search Interest
Python
This source shows search interest in Python, one of the most commonly used programming languages in data science, machine learning, and AI. In the project, Python can be used as a general indicator of public interest in data and programming skills.
LLM
This source shows search interest in “LLM,” which stands for large language model. This term is useful for studying recent interest in generative AI systems and language-based AI tools.
Gen AI
This source shows search interest in the shorter term “Gen AI.” It can be compared with “generative AI” to see how different wording may capture public interest in the same broader topic.
AI agents
This source shows search interest in “AI agents,” a newer AI-related term. It can help us examine whether interest is shifting from general AI tools toward more advanced AI systems that can perform tasks more independently.
Open AI
This source shows search interest in “Open AI.” It can be used as a public-interest indicator for one of the major organizations associated with recent AI tools. However, we should be careful because search interest in a company name may reflect news attention as well as career or skill interest.
Deep learning
This source shows search interest in “deep learning,” an important AI method used in neural networks, computer vision, natural language processing, and generative AI. It can help us compare older AI-related terminology with newer terms such as LLM and generative AI.
RAG system
This source shows search interest in “RAG system,” which refers to retrieval-augmented generation. This is a more specialized AI term and may be useful for examining whether newer technical AI skills are gaining public attention.

The rapid growth of generative AI raises important questions about how AI adoption is reflected in labor-market demand, especially for data analytics and software roles. This analysis examines whether public interest, technology market signals, technology investment, and macroeconomic indicators help explain and forecast changes in job openings.
Research questions

How do data analytics (DA) and software (SW) job openings differ from overall U.S. job openings (ALL) in their relationship with macroeconomic and technology investment indicators?
Can public interest and technology investment signals help predict changes in job-market demand for AI- and data-related roles?

Workflow

Part 1 – Exploratory analysis (daily): time-series plots, linear regression, and cross-correlation (CCF) in levels and first differences.

read_file <- function(filename) {

  data <- read_csv(file.path(data_folder, filename), show_col_types = FALSE)

  # Find the date column
  date_col <- names(data)[grepl("date|month|time", names(data), ignore.case = TRUE)][1]

  if (is.na(date_col)) {
    stop("No date column found in: ", filename)
  }

  # Parse dates in any of the common formats
  date_values <- as.character(data[[date_col]])

  parsed_dates <- suppressWarnings(
    as.Date(
      parse_date_time(
        date_values,
        orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy", "ym", "my", "Ymd", "bY", "BY",
                   "bdy", "Ymd HMS", "ymd HMS")
      )
    )
  )

  if (all(is.na(parsed_dates))) {
    stop("Dates could not be read in: ", filename,
         "\nFirst date values: ", paste(head(date_values), collapse = ", "))
  }

  names(data)[names(data) == date_col] <- "Date"
  data$Date <- parsed_dates

  # Prefix all other columns with the file name
  file_prefix <- make.names(tools::file_path_sans_ext(filename))

  data %>%
    filter(!is.na(Date)) %>%
    rename_with(~ paste0(file_prefix, "_", .x), -Date)
}

3.3 Build a regularly spaced daily dataset
Stock prices are only observed on trading days, so the merged data are placed on a complete daily calendar (duplicate dates are averaged). Two versions are created:

ccf_data: only internal gaps are linearly interpolated (used for CCF).
model_data: all gaps are filled with forecast::na.interp() (used for regression and forecasting models).



Code
needed_columns <- unique(c("Date", unname(job_columns), unname(predictor_columns)))

daily_data <- combined_data %>%
  select(all_of(needed_columns)) %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ if (all(is.na(.x))) NA_real_ else mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  complete(Date = seq(min(Date), max(Date), by = "day")) %>%
  arrange(Date)

# Interpolate internal gaps only (no extrapolation at the ends)
interpolate_daily <- function(x, dates) {
  available <- !is.na(x)
  if (sum(available) < 2) return(x)
  approx(
    x = as.numeric(dates[available]), y = x[available],
    xout = as.numeric(dates), rule = 1
  )$y
}

ccf_data <- daily_data %>%
  mutate(across(-Date, ~ interpolate_daily(.x, Date)))

model_data <- daily_data %>%
  mutate(across(-Date, ~ as.numeric(forecast::na.interp(.x))))

tibble(
  Dataset = c("ccf_data", "model_data"),
  Days    = c(nrow(ccf_data), nrow(model_data)),
  Missing_values = c(sum(is.na(ccf_data[-1])), sum(is.na(model_data[-1])))
) %>%

plot_jobs_with <- function(pred_lookup, pred_title, pred_subtitle,
                           pred_color, figure_title) {

  lookup <- bind_rows(
    job_lookup  %>% mutate(Group = "Job Openings"),
    pred_lookup %>% mutate(Group = "Predictors")
  )

  long_data <- daily_data %>%
    select(Date, all_of(lookup$Column)) %>%
    pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = "Column", values_to = "Value") %>%
    left_join(lookup, by = "Column") %>%
    filter(!is.na(Value)) %>%
    mutate(Series = factor(Series, levels = unique(lookup$Series)))

  date_limits <- range(long_data$Date)

  make_panel <- function(group, color, title, subtitle, show_x) {
    long_data %>%
      filter(Group == group) %>%
      ggplot(aes(Date, Value)) +
      geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, color = color) +
      facet_grid(Series ~ ., scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
      scale_x_date(limits = date_limits, date_breaks = "6 months",
                   date_labels = "%b %Y", expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)) +
      labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle,
           x = if (show_x) "Date" else NULL, y = NULL) +
      theme_ts() +
      theme(
        strip.placement   = "outside",
        strip.background  = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, face = "bold", size = 9),
        axis.text.x       = if (show_x) element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1) else element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x      = if (show_x) element_line() else element_blank()
      )
  }

  top <- make_panel("Job Openings", col_actual, "Job Openings",
                    "Daily posting indices for data analysis, software, and all jobs",
                    show_x = FALSE)

  bottom <- make_panel("Predictors", pred_color, pred_title, pred_subtitle,
                       show_x = TRUE)

  (top / bottom) +
    plot_layout(heights = c(3, nrow(pred_lookup))) +
    plot_annotation(
      title = figure_title,
      subtitle = "Each panel uses its own vertical scale; all panels share the same time axis",
      theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20),
                    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray35"))
    )
}

4.2 Linear regression
As a first look at explanatory power, each job-opening series is regressed on each predictor group separately (contemporaneous values, no time-series error structure). Because these are trending series, the R² values describe co-movement and should not be read as causal effects; residual autocorrelation is addressed in Parts 2 and 3.

fit_models <- function(predictors) {
  lapply(job_columns, function(outcome) {
    model_formula <- as.formula(
      paste0("`", outcome, "` ~ ", paste0("`", unname(predictors), "`", collapse = " + "))
    )
    lm(model_formula, data = model_data)
  })
}

regression_models <- list(
  "Google Trends" = fit_models(google_columns),
  "Stock Prices"  = fit_models(stock_columns),
  "CAPEX and PPI" = fit_models(capex_ppi_columns)
)

regression_results <- imap_dfr(regression_models, function(models, group) {
  imap_dfr(models, function(model, job) {
    fit <- glance(model)
    tibble(
      Predictor_Group = group,
      Job_Openings    = job_labels[[job]],
      R_Squared       = fit$r.squared,
      Adj_R_Squared   = fit$adj.r.squared,
      RMSE            = sqrt(mean(residuals(model)^2)),
      AIC             = fit$AIC,
      N               = nobs(model)
    )
  })
})

text:
4.3 Cross-correlation analysis (CCF)
We use the CCF to examine lead–lag dependence between job openings and each external signal. The sample CCF at lag \(k\) estimates \(\text{cor}(\text{Job}_{t+k}, X_t)\), so:

positive lags → the predictor leads job openings,
negative lags → job openings lead the predictor,
lag 0 → same-day relationship.

Approximate 95% significance limits are \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\).






Important



CCF on raw levels can be misleading. When two series are trending or nonstationary, they can appear strongly correlated at every lag simply because they share a trend. We therefore report the CCF on levels for completeness, and then on first-differenced series (daily changes), which is the more reliable basis for identifying lead–lag structure. Prewhitening is a further refinement.




Code
compute_ccf <- function(data, lag_max) {

  results <- list()

  for (job_name in names(job_columns)) {
    for (predictor_name in names(predictor_columns)) {

      pair <- data %>%
        select(job  = all_of(job_columns[[job_name]]),
               pred = all_of(predictor_columns[[predictor_name]])) %>%
        drop_na()

      if (nrow(pair) > lag_max + 2 && sd(pair$job) > 0 && sd(pair$pred) > 0) {

        cc <- ccf(pair$job, pair$pred, lag.max = lag_max, plot = FALSE)

        results[[length(results) + 1]] <- tibble(
          Category        = predictor_groups[[predictor_name]],
          Job_Openings    = job_name,
          Predictor       = predictor_name,
          Lag             = as.numeric(cc$lag),
          CCF             = as.numeric(cc$acf),
          N               = nrow(pair),
          Approx_95_Bound = 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(pair))
        )
      }
    }
  }

  bind_rows(results) %>%
    mutate(Significant = abs(CCF) > Approx_95_Bound)
}

label_ccf <- function(ccf_df) {
  ccf_df %>%
    mutate(
      Job_Type = factor(
        recode(Job_Openings, DA = "Data Analysis", SW = "Software Development",
               ALL = "All Job Openings"),
        levels = c("All Job Openings", "Data Analysis", "Software Development")
      ),
      Predictor_Label = case_when(
        Category == "Google Trends" ~ clean_gt_label(Predictor),
        Predictor == "MSFT"  ~ "Microsoft (MSFT)",
        Predictor == "C3AI"  ~ "C3.ai (AI)",
        Predictor == "NVDA"  ~ "NVIDIA (NVDA)",
        Predictor == "GOOGL" ~ "Alphabet (GOOGL)",
        grepl("PCU|PPI", Predictor, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "PPI (Information)",
        grepl("CAPEX",   Predictor, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "CAPEX",
        TRUE ~ Predictor
      ),
      Category = factor(Category, levels = c("Google Trends", "Stock Prices", "CAPEX and PPI"))
    )
}

# Strongest absolute CCF for each job x predictor pair
ccf_peaks <- function(ccf_df) {
  ccf_df %>%
    group_by(Category, Job_Type, Predictor_Label) %>%
    slice_max(abs(CCF), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(
      Lag_Interpretation = case_when(
        Lag > 0 ~ "Predictor leads job openings",
        Lag < 0 ~ "Job openings lead predictor",
        TRUE    ~ "Same-day relationship"
      )
    ) %>%
    arrange(Category, Job_Type, desc(abs(CCF))) %>%
    select(Category, Job_Type, Predictor = Predictor_Label, Lag, CCF,
           Approx_95_Bound, Significant, Lag_Interpretation)
}

# Heatmap of all CCF values
ccf_heatmap <- function(ccf_df, title, subtitle) {
  ggplot(ccf_df, aes(Lag, Predictor_Label, fill = CCF)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
    facet_grid(Category ~ Job_Type, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3B4CC0", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#B40426",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), oob = squish,
                         breaks = seq(-1, 1, 0.5), name = "CCF") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-20, 20, 10), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = "Lag in days", y = NULL,
         caption = paste0("Blue = negative, red = positive correlation. ",
                          "Positive lags indicate that the external indicator leads job openings.")) +
    theme_ts() +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
          strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold"),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5),
          legend.position = "right")
}

# Stem plots; significant lags are highlighted
ccf_stem_plot <- function(ccf_df, title, subtitle, facet = c("grid", "wrap")) {

  facet  <- match.arg(facet)
  bounds <- ccf_df %>% distinct(Job_Type, Predictor_Label, Approx_95_Bound)

  p <- ggplot(ccf_df, aes(Lag, CCF)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_hline(data = bounds, aes(yintercept =  Approx_95_Bound),
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.45, color = "steelblue") +
    geom_hline(data = bounds, aes(yintercept = -Approx_95_Bound),
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.45, color = "steelblue") +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = Lag, y = 0, yend = CCF, color = Significant), linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#3B4CC0", `FALSE` = "gray65"),
                       labels = c(`TRUE` = "Outside 95% limits", `FALSE` = "Within limits"),
                       name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-lag_max, lag_max, 10)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = "Lag in days",
         y = "Cross-correlation coefficient",
         caption = paste0("Dashed lines show approximate 95% limits. ",
                          "Positive lags indicate that the predictor leads job openings.")) +
    theme_ts()

  if (facet == "grid") {
    p + facet_grid(rows = vars(Job_Type), cols = vars(Predictor_Label))
  } else {
    p + facet_wrap(~ Predictor_Label, ncol = 3)
  }
}

Daily series are modelled with weekly seasonality (frequency = 7). The regression-with-ARIMA-error models use the observed predictor values in the test period (ex-post forecasts), so they measure how much the predictors explain out of sample rather than a fully operational forecast.


Code
# Fit on the training window and predict the test window.
# Returns the model plus fitted (training) and predicted (test) values.
fit_and_forecast <- function(y, xreg = NULL, h = test_horizon) {

  n         <- length(y)
  train_end <- n - h
  y_train   <- ts(y[1:train_end], frequency = 7)

  if (is.null(xreg)) {
    model <- auto.arima(y_train, seasonal = TRUE,
                        stepwise = !exhaustive_search, approximation = !exhaustive_search)
    fc <- forecast(model, h = h, level = 95)
  } else {
    xreg <- as.matrix(xreg)
    storage.mode(xreg) <- "double"
    model <- auto.arima(y_train, xreg = xreg[1:train_end, , drop = FALSE],
                        seasonal = TRUE, stepwise = !exhaustive_search, approximation = !exhaustive_search)
    fc <- forecast(model, xreg = xreg[(train_end + 1):n, , drop = FALSE], level = 95)
  }

  list(
    model = model,
    results = tibble(
      Actual           = y,
      Fitted_Predicted = c(as.numeric(fitted(model)), as.numeric(fc$mean)),
      Lower_95         = c(rep(NA_real_, train_end), as.numeric(fc$lower[, 1])),
      Upper_95         = c(rep(NA_real_, train_end), as.numeric(fc$upper[, 1])),
      Period           = rep(c("Training", "Test"), c(train_end, h))
    )
  )
}

# Actual vs predicted plot: test period only, or the whole series
plot_actual_vs_predicted <- function(pred_df, title, subtitle, whole = FALSE) {

  pred_name  <- if (whole) "Fitted / Predicted" else "Predicted"
  test_start <- min(pred_df$Date[pred_df$Period == "Test"])
  df         <- if (whole) pred_df else filter(pred_df, Period == "Test")

  long_df <- df %>%
    select(Date, Job_Type, Actual, Fitted_Predicted) %>%
    pivot_longer(c(Actual, Fitted_Predicted), names_to = "Series", values_to = "Value") %>%
    mutate(Series = if_else(Series == "Actual", "Actual", pred_name))

  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Date))

  if (!whole) {
    p <- p + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower_95, ymax = Upper_95),
                         fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.35)
  } else {
    p <- p + geom_vline(xintercept = test_start, color = "gray40",
                        linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.7)
  }

  p +
    geom_line(data = long_df, aes(y = Value, color = Series, linetype = Series),
              linewidth = if (whole) 0.6 else 0.9) +
    facet_grid(Job_Type ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
    scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c(col_actual, col_pred), c("Actual", pred_name))) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = setNames(c("solid", "dashed"), c("Actual", pred_name))) +
    labs(
      title = title, subtitle = subtitle,
      x = "Date", y = "Job-posting index", color = NULL, linetype = NULL,
      caption = if (whole) {
        "Dashed line: fitted values (training) and predictions (test). Dotted vertical line marks the start of the test period."
      } else {
        paste0("The final ", test_horizon, " days were used as the test period. Shaded regions are 95% prediction intervals.")
      }
    ) +
    theme_ts()
}

5.4.2 Diebold–Mariano tests against the ARIMA baseline
The Diebold–Mariano (DM) test checks whether the squared-error loss of each external-predictor model differs significantly from the univariate ARIMA baseline over the test period. Because all test forecasts come from a single forecast origin (horizons 1 to 36), the test is used here as a descriptive guide rather than a formal multi-origin comparison.


Code
baseline_errors <- all_predictions %>%
  filter(Period == "Test", Model == "ARIMA (baseline)") %>%
  transmute(Date, Job_Type, Baseline_Error = Actual - Fitted_Predicted)

dm_results <- all_predictions %>%
  filter(Period == "Test", Model != "ARIMA (baseline)") %>%
  transmute(Date, Job_Type, Model, Model_Error = Actual - Fitted_Predicted) %>%
  inner_join(baseline_errors, by = c("Date", "Job_Type")) %>%
  group_by(Job_Type, Model) %>%
  summarise(
    {
      dm <- forecast::dm.test(Baseline_Error, Model_Error,
                              alternative = "two.sided", h = 1, power = 2)
      tibble(DM_Statistic = unname(dm$statistic), P_Value = dm$p.value)
    },
    Lower_Loss = if_else(mean(Model_Error^2) < mean(Baseline_Error^2),
                         as.character(first(Model)), "ARIMA (baseline)"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Significant = if_else(P_Value < 0.05, "Yes", "No"))

SARIMA.c <- function(p1, p2, q1, q2, P1, P2, Q1, Q2, data, d = 0, D = 1, s = 12) {

  results <- list()

  for (p in p1:p2) for (q in q1:q2) for (P in P1:P2) for (Q in Q1:Q2) {

    if (p + d + q + P + D + Q <= 10) {

      model <- tryCatch(
        Arima(data, order = c(p, d, q),
              seasonal = list(order = c(P, D, Q), period = s)),
        error = function(e) NULL
      )

          p = p, d = d, q = q, P = P, D = D, Q = Q,
          AIC = model$aic, BIC = model$bic, AICc = model$aicc
        )
      }
    }
  }

  if (length(results) == 0) stop("No SARIMA models were successfully fitted.")
  bind_rows(results)

6.6 Time-series cross-validation
The two seasonal candidates are compared with an expanding-window cross-validation. The initial training window is roughly one-third of the sample (rounded down to whole years), and 12-month-ahead forecasts are produced at every origin.


Code
y_cv <- res.fit
n    <- length(y_cv)
k    <- floor(n / 3 / 12) * 12   # initial training window
h    <- 12                       # forecast horizon (months)

n_origins <- n - k - h + 1

if (k < 24)        warning("The initial training window contains fewer than two seasonal cycles.")
if (n_origins < 1) stop("There are not enough observations for 12-step cross-validation.")

cv_models <- list(
  "SARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1)[12]" = list(order = c(1, 0, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1)),
  "SARIMA(1,0,1)(1,1,1)[12]" = list(order = c(1, 0, 1), seasonal = c(1, 1, 1))
)

cv_errors <- lapply(cv_models, function(x) matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_origins, ncol = h))

for (i in seq_len(n_origins)) {

  train_end <- k + i - 1
  xtrain    <- window(y_cv, end = time(y_cv)[train_end])
  xtest     <- as.numeric(y_cv[(train_end + 1):(train_end + h)])

  for (model_name in names(cv_models)) {
    spec <- cv_models[[model_name]]
    fit_i <- tryCatch(
      Arima(xtrain, order = spec$order,
            seasonal = list(order = spec$seasonal, period = 12), method = "ML"),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (!is.null(fit_i)) {
      cv_errors[[model_name]][i, ] <- as.numeric(forecast(fit_i, h = h)$mean) - xtest
    }
  }
}

  bind_cols(map_dfc(cv_errors, ~ sqrt(colMeans(.x^2, na.rm = TRUE))))

6.9 Forecasting
Each exogenous variable is first forecast with its own auto.arima model; those forecasts are then used as future regressors for the ARIMAX forecast of DA job postings.


Code
monthly_h <- 36

fxreg <- sapply(c("FedFundsRate", "PCE", "PPIInformation"), function(var_name) {
  as.numeric(forecast(auto.arima(xreg[, var_name]), h = monthly_h)$mean)
})

fcast <- forecast(fit, xreg = fxreg, h = monthly_h)
